added: Electric generators are devices that use alternating magnetic fields to create a current through a wire circuit. While full scale models can be complex and expensive to build, you can create a simple electric generator easily. All you need to do is create a simple frame to hold the wire and magnet, wind the wire, connect it to an electrical device, and glue the magnet onto a spinning shaft. This works well to teach electromagnetic properties, or display as a science project.

added: Electric generators are devices that use alternating magnetic fields to create a current through a wire circuit. While full scale models can be complex and expensive to build, you can create a simple electric generator easily. All you need to do is create a simple frame to hold the wire and magnet, wind the wire, connect it to an electrical device, and glue the magnet onto a spinning shaft. This even works well to teach electromagnetic properties, or display as a science project.
[[Category:Electrical Projects]]
[[Category:Motors Generators and Transformers]]
== Steps ==
===Building the Frame===

#Cut the [[Cut-Thick-Cardboard|cardboard]]. Cardboard will serve as the frame and support for your simple generator. [[Use-a-Ruler|Use a ruler]] to measure a cardboard strip that is {{convert|8|cm|in}} by {{convert|30.4|cm|in|}}. Cut this strip out with scissors or a utility knife. This single piece will be folded to form the frame.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k7Sz8oT8ou0</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 1 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Mark the cardboard. Use a ruler to measure along the length of the cardboard. Make your first mark at {{convert|8|cm|in}}. Your second mark should be at {{convert|11.5|cm|in}}, and your third mark should be at {{convert|19.5|cm|in}}. The final mark will be at {{convert|22.7|cm|in}}.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k7Sz8oT8ou0</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 2 Version 4.jpg|center]]
#*This creates segments of {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.5|cm|in}}, {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.2|cm|in}}, and {{convert|7.7|cm|in}}. Do not cut these segments.

#Fold the cardboard. Fold the cardboard along each mark. This will make your flat piece of cardboard into a rectangular frame. This frame will house the components of your electric motor.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 3 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Slide the metal shaft through the support frame. Push a nail through the center of the cardboard frame. Make sure you go through all three pieces of cardboard that are folded into the center. This will create the hole for your shaft. You can now insert a metal shaft, or use the nail as your shaft.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k7Sz8oT8ou0</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 4 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#*The metal shaft does not have to be anything in particular. Any piece of metal that will fit through the hole and come all the way out the other side of the frame is acceptable. The nail you use to make the hole will work perfectly.
===Creating the Circuit===

#Wind the copper wire. Make several turns around the cardboard box with enamel coated copper wire (#30 magnet wire). Wind {{convert|200|ft|m|}} of wire as tight as you can. Leave about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your meter, light bulb, or other electronic device. The more "turns" or winds you make around the cardboard frame, the more power your generator should produce.<ref>https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k7Sz8oT8ou0</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 5 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Strip the ends of the wire. Use a knife or a [[Use-Wire-Strippers|wire stripper]] to remove the insulation from each end of the wire. Remove about {{convert|2.54|cm|in|}} of insulation from each side. This will allow you to connect the wire to an electronic device.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 6 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Connect the wires to an electronic device. Attach the two wires you have loose at the ends of the windings to a red LED, #49 miniature bulb, or a 1.5V grain-of-wheat lamp. Or, connect the test leads from an AC [[Use-a-Voltmeter|voltmeter]] or [[Use-a-Digital-Multimeter|multimeter]] to them. Keep in mind that you are producing a very low [[Measure-Voltage|voltage]], and larger devices (e.g. a regular light bulb) will not be powered by this generator.<ref>https://van.physics.illinois.edu/ask/listing/574</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 7 Version 5.jpg|center]]
===Setting the Magnets===

#Glue the magnets to the shaft. Use a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy to glue four ceramic magnets to the shaft. You want the magnet to be stationary with respect to the shaft. The magnets should be glued onto the shaft after the shaft has been inserted into the frame. Allow the glue to dry for several minutes (the instructions on the container can tell you exact drying times for your type of glue).<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 8 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*For best results, use 1x2x5 cm ceramic magnets (these can be found online for a reasonable price). Glue them so that two magnets are facing the coil with their north side, and two are facing the coil with their south side.

#Turn the shaft with your fingers. This allows you to see if the ends of the magnets hit the inside of the frame. The magnets must turn freely, but as close as possible to the walls of the frame. Again, having the magnet's ends as close the copper wire windings as possible will increase the "exciting" action of the magnetic fields the magnet produces.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 9 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Spin the shaft as fast as possible. You may want to wind a string around the end of the shaft, then pull it sharply to turn the magnets. You could even just spin it with your fingers. As the shaft turns, you should get a small voltage (enough to light a 1.5 volt light bulb).<ref>https://van.physics.illinois.edu/ask/listing/574</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 10 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*You could improve the power output by putting a pinwheel on the end of the shaft and connecting it to an electric fan to turn the wheel. Keep in mind that this is only good to demonstrate the operation of the generator since you use more electricity turning it than you create.

===Building the Frame===

#Cut the cardboard. Cardboard will serve as the frame and support for your simple generator. Use a ruler to measure a cardboard strip that is {{convert|8|cm|in}} by {{convert|30.4|cm|in|}}. #Slide the metal shaft through the support frame. Push a nail through the center of the cardboard frame. Make sure you go through all three pieces of cardboard that are folded into the center. added: Electric generators are devices that use alternating magnetic fields to create a current through a wire circuit. While full scale models can be complex and expensive to build, you can create a simple electric generator easily. All you need to do is create a simple frame to hold the wire and magnet, wind the wire, connect it to an electrical device, and glue the magnet onto a spinning shaft. This even works well to teach electromagnetic properties, or display as a science project.
[[Category:Electrical Projects]]
[[Category:Motors Generators and Transformers]]
== Steps ==
===Building the Frame===

#Cut the cardboard. Cardboard will serve as the frame and support for your simple generator. Use a ruler to measure a cardboard strip that is {{convert|8|cm|in}} by {{convert|30.4|cm|in|}}. Cut this strip out with scissors or a utility knife. This single piece will be folded to form the frame.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 1 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Mark the cardboard. Use a ruler to measure along the length of the cardboard. Make your first mark at {{convert|8|cm|in}}. Your second mark should be at {{convert|11.5|cm|in}}, and your third mark should be at {{convert|19.5|cm|in}}. The final mark will be at {{convert|22.7|cm|in}}.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 2 Version 4.jpg|center]]
#*This creates segments of {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.5|cm|in}}, {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.2|cm|in}}, and {{convert|7.7|cm|in}}. Do not cut these segments.

#Fold the cardboard. Fold the cardboard along each mark. This will make your flat piece of cardboard into a rectangular frame. This frame will house the components of your electric motor.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 3 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Slide the metal shaft through the support frame. Push a nail through the center of the cardboard frame. Make sure you go through all three pieces of cardboard that are folded into the center. This will create the hole for your shaft. You can now insert a metal shaft, or use the nail as your shaft.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#07</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 4 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#*The metal shaft does not have to be anything in particular. Any piece of metal that will fit through the hole and come all the way out the other side of the frame is acceptable. The nail you use to make the hole will work perfectly.
===Creating the Circuit===

#Wind the copper wire. Make several turns around the cardboard box with enamel coated copper wire (#30 magnet wire). Wind {{convert|200|ft|m|}} of wire as tight as you can. Leave about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your meter, light bulb, or other electronic device. The more "turns" or winds you make around the cardboard frame, the more power your generator should produce.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 5 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Strip the ends of the wire. Use a knife or a wire stripper to remove the insulation from each end of the wire. Remove about {{convert|2.54|cm|in|}} of insulation from each side. This will allow you to connect the wire to an electronic device.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 6 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Connect the wires to an electronic device. Attach the two wires you have loose at the ends of the windings to a red LED, #49 miniature bulb, or a 1.5V grain-of-wheat lamp. Or, connect the test leads from an AC voltmeter or multimeter to them. Keep in mind that you are producing a very low voltage, and larger devices (e.g. a regular light bulb) will not be powered by this generator.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 7 Version 5.jpg|center]]
===Setting the Magnets===

#Glue the magnets to the shaft. Use a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy to glue four ceramic magnets to the shaft. You want the magnet to be stationary with respect to the shaft. The magnets should be glued onto the shaft after the shaft has been inserted into the frame. Allow the glue to dry for several minutes (the instructions on the container can tell you exact drying times for your type of glue).<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 8 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*For best results, use 1x2x5 cm ceramic magnets (these can be found online for a reasonable price). Glue them so that two magnets are facing the coil with their north side, and two are facing the coil with their south side.

#Turn the shaft with your fingers. This allows you to see if the ends of the magnets hit the inside of the frame. The magnets must turn freely, but as close as possible to the walls of the frame. Again, having the magnet's ends as close the copper wire windings as possible will increase the "exciting" action of the magnetic fields the magnet produces.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 9 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Spin the shaft as fast as possible. You may want to wind a string around the end of the shaft, then pull it sharply to turn the magnets. You could even just spin it with your fingers. As the shaft turns, you should get a small voltage (enough to light a 1.5 volt light bulb).<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 10 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*You could improve the power output by putting a pinwheel on the end of the shaft and connecting it to an electric fan to turn the wheel. Keep in mind that this is only good to demonstrate the operation of the generator since you use more electricity turning it than you create.
== Video ==
{{Video:Make a Simple Electric Generator|}}
== Things You'll Need ==
* #30 Magnet wire
* Four 1x2x5 cm ceramic magnets
* Thick nail or shaft
* Cardboard box
* Multimeter or electrical device

removed: You will be forgiven for not spending the majority of your days thinking about the concept of electromagnetic induction and the anatomy of a diesel generator. After all, we all have better things to do, such as working, playing, cooking, cleaning, studying, and any other leisurely activity. However, with one closer look, we instantly come to the realization that all these aforementioned activities are dependent on our use of technology, and this is why having a bit more grasp on the subject of “backup power generators” wouldn’t be the worst thing in the world

After all, when a power blackout inevitably happens, the first thing we’ll hope to have is a backup power source in place, and when you have the requisite knowledge about the genset available, choosing the ideal unit becomes that much easier. But as soon as you jog to the market in search of your dream generator, you’ll be shocked to witness the sheer range of units available at your disposal, which is both a blessing and a challenge.

Diesel generators have been around forever, and still find a prominent place in our industries because they simply are incredible at their job, which is to derive electrical energy and power electronic appliances for as long as the primary grid is out. Now that it has been established that the diesel genset is the real deal, choosing one as per your personal requirement is the next major step. To help you in the pursuit, we are going to categorize different types of [https://krugerpower.com.au/diesel-generators.html   diesel generators ] (and later fuel-generators) based on different factors.
# Diesel Generators Based On-
a) Number of Strokes:
1. 2-stroke Generators: A complete power cycle refers to one full stroke. So ina 2-stroke mechanism, the cycle is concluded within two strokes, where the engine crankshaft revolves only one time.

2. 4-Stroke Generators: Naturally, here one full power cycle is completed in 4 strokes of the piston, and the engine crankshaft revolves twice during that full cycle. Other less common variants are 5-stroke, 6-stroke, etc generator sets.
b) Load-Bearing:

1. Standby Power DG: The engine for this generator type will not be operating for more than 100 hours in total in a single year, and will not exceed 80% of the [https://www.pgsys.com.au/faq/what-do-the-various-generator-ratings-mean/   power rating ] for the whole duration of the power outage.

2. Prime Power DG: In this type, the engine is able to run for an unlimited number of years throughout the year, and that too at 100% of prime power rating. With that said, the overall load on the engine should not be more than 70% of the power rating here.

3. Continuous Power DG: As the name suggests, the engine for this generator can also operate continuously for an unlimited number of hours throughout the year at 100% of its power rating. The engine load can vary anywhere between 70% - 100% of the power rating.
c) Type Of Cooling System.

1. Air-Cooled DG: This type of diesel generator will use atmospheric air as a cooling agent (coolant) to prevent overheating of the engine parts. This system is better suited to small-sized portable diesel generators with small running durations (a few hours).

2. Fluid/Water-Cooled DG: This type of generator makes use of water injection (or oil/lubricant) to cool down the hated parts. This generator requires a radiator and the system is installed in large-sized commercial diesel generators with high-load applications.
d) Starting Method.
1. Automatic Starting DG: The engine operating mechanism here is dependent on electrical, hydraulic, and air-camshaft starting systems.

2. Manually Starting DG: These generators will not have a pre-defined start-up time and duration of running. The user himself will have to be present there in order to get the generator running. Manually barring engines are most common in houses.
e) Motor Speed.
1. Low-Speed DG: Larger the machine, lower the motor speed. So these large machines run at the motor speed of 150-450 RPM (Rotations Per Minute).
2. Medium Speed DG: Medium-sized generators of this kind will operate at a motor speed of 500-1200 RPM.
3. High-Speed DG: Small, compact portable generators are included in this category and they have a motor rotational speed of around 1500-2000 RPM.
# 5 Most Popular Fuel-Based Generators Ranked in 2021:-
1. Diesel Generators:

The undisputed kingpin amongst all types of generators, diesel generators have had the biggest impact on the industry that we see today. Diesel is more readily available than any other fuel source, and is also comparatively cost-effective, thereby making diesel generators the obvious candidates of widespread acceptance.

Also, these generators offer long life-spans, load-bearing capabilities, high resale value, lower upkeep (maintenance) needs, etc. Their fuel consumption chart denotes how brilliant fuel efficiency they possess as well. So its really easy to see why every genset brand owner and their pets prefer diesel generators, especially the ones supplied by the leading experts such as [https://ablegen.com.au/   AbleGen ] for both business and personal power requirements.
2. Gasoline (Petrol) Generators:

Petrol, to its credit, is also very readily available. However, that’s not the case during a crisis situation where the prices go sky high and you’re left with a petrol generator in reach, but not the fuel to keep it running. Even then, petrol generators are also quite common due to their low-end on the cost scale. These generators are affordable and offer a sufficient enough power supply.
3. Natural Gas Generators:

In the wake of recent climate discussions, Natural Gas generators have also emerged as a viable choice. Although not the most power-efficient, these generators are more eco-friendly than their other counterparts since they employ natural gas as a source of fuel. But if you have large power supply needs, or are facing prolonged power outages, then perhaps (NG) generators are not going to fill you with too much confidence.
4. Propane Gas Generators:

Propane Gas generators, obviously, use propane as the fuel source (whether in liquid or gaseous form) to generate electricity. Propane fuel burns cleaner than most, and is also affordable. However, once again, availability is an issue when it comes to facing a climatic crisis.
5: Bio-diesel Generators:

[https://www.biodiesel.org/what-is-biodiesel/biodiesel-basics   Bio-diesel ] is a mixture of diesel fuel with any other biological fuel, such as vegetable oil or animal fat oil. Bio-diesel as fuel is, therefore, more environmentally friendly than using just diesel, while compromising with some of the power efficiency aspects of the latter. Bio-diesel generators are not very common to find, and their life-expectancy can generally be very hit or miss.

After all, when a power blackout inevitably happens, the first thing we’ll hope to have is a backup power source in place, and when you have the requisite knowledge about the genset available, choosing the ideal unit becomes that much easier. But as soon as you jog to the market in search of your dream generator, you’ll be shocked to witness the sheer range of units available at your disposal, which is both a blessing and a challenge.

Diesel generators have been around forever, and still find a prominent place in our industries because they simply are incredible at their job, which is to derive electrical energy and power electronic appliances for as long as the primary grid is out. Now that it has been established that the diesel genset is the real deal, choosing one as per your personal requirement is the next major step. To help you in the pursuit, we are going to categorize different types of '''diesel generators'''[[https://krugerpower.com.au/diesel-generators.html]] (and later fuel-generators) based on different factors.
# Diesel Generators Based On-
a) Number of Strokes:
1. 2-stroke Generators: A complete power cycle refers to one full stroke. So ina 2-stroke mechanism, the cycle is concluded within two strokes, where the engine crankshaft revolves only one time.

2. 4-Stroke Generators: Naturally, here one full power cycle is completed in 4 strokes of the piston, and the engine crankshaft revolves twice during that full cycle. Other less common variants are 5-stroke, 6-stroke, etc generator sets.
b) Load-Bearing:

1. Standby Power DG: The engine for this generator type will not be operating for more than 100 hours in total in a single year, and will not exceed 80% of the '''power rating'''[[https://www.pgsys.com.au/faq/what-do-the-various-generator-ratings-mean/]] for the whole duration of the power outage.

2. Prime Power DG: In this type, the engine is able to run for an unlimited number of years throughout the year, and that too at 100% of prime power rating. With that said, the overall load on the engine should not be more than 70% of the power rating here.

3. Continuous Power DG: As the name suggests, the engine for this generator can also operate continuously for an unlimited number of hours throughout the year at 100% of its power rating. The engine load can vary anywhere between 70% - 100% of the power rating.
c) Type Of Cooling System.

1. Air-Cooled DG: This type of diesel generator will use atmospheric air as a cooling agent (coolant) to prevent overheating of the engine parts. This system is better suited to small-sized portable diesel generators with small running durations (a few hours).

2. Fluid/Water-Cooled DG: This type of generator makes use of water injection (or oil/lubricant) to cool down the hated parts. This generator requires a radiator and the system is installed in large-sized commercial diesel generators with high-load applications.
d) Starting Method.
1. Automatic Starting DG: The engine operating mechanism here is dependent on electrical, hydraulic, and air-camshaft starting systems.

2. Manually Starting DG: These generators will not have a pre-defined start-up time and duration of running. The user himself will have to be present there in order to get the generator running. Manually barring engines are most common in houses.
e) Motor Speed.
1. Low-Speed DG: Larger the machine, lower the motor speed. So these large machines run at the motor speed of 150-450 RPM (Rotations Per Minute).
2. Medium Speed DG: Medium-sized generators of this kind will operate at a motor speed of 500-1200 RPM.
3. High-Speed DG: Small, compact portable generators are included in this category and they have a motor rotational speed of around 1500-2000 RPM.
# 5 Most Popular Fuel-Based Generators Ranked in 2021:-
1. Diesel Generators:

The undisputed kingpin amongst all types of generators, diesel generators have had the biggest impact on the industry that we see today. Diesel is more readily available than any other fuel source, and is also comparatively cost-effective, thereby making diesel generators the obvious candidates of widespread acceptance.

Also, these generators offer long life-spans, load-bearing capabilities, high resale value, lower upkeep (maintenance) needs, etc. Their fuel consumption chart denotes how brilliant fuel efficiency they possess as well. So its really easy to see why every genset brand owner and their pets prefer diesel generators, especially the ones supplied by the leading experts such as '''AbleGen'''[[https://ablegen.com.au/]] for both business and personal power requirements.
2. Gasoline (Petrol) Generators:

Petrol, to its credit, is also very readily available. However, that’s not the case during a crisis situation where the prices go sky high and you’re left with a petrol generator in reach, but not the fuel to keep it running. Even then, petrol generators are also quite common due to their low-end on the cost scale. These generators are affordable and offer a sufficient enough power supply.
3. Natural Gas Generators:

In the wake of recent climate discussions, Natural Gas generators have also emerged as a viable choice. Although not the most power-efficient, these generators are more eco-friendly than their other counterparts since they employ natural gas as a source of fuel. But if you have large power supply needs, or are facing prolonged power outages, then perhaps (NG) generators are not going to fill you with too much confidence.
4. Propane Gas Generators:

Propane Gas generators, obviously, use propane as the fuel source (whether in liquid or gaseous form) to generate electricity. Propane fuel burns cleaner than most, and is also affordable. However, once again, availability is an issue when it comes to facing a climatic crisis.
5: Bio-diesel Generators:

Bio-diesel is a mixture of diesel fuel with any other biological fuel, such as vegetable oil or animal fat oil. Bio-diesel as fuel is, therefore, more environmentally friendly than using just diesel, while compromising with some of the power efficiency aspects of the latter. Bio-diesel generators are not very common to find, and their life-expectancy can generally be very hit or miss.

removed: Electric generators are devices that use alternating magnetic fields to create a current through a wire circuit. While full scale models can be complex and expensive to build, you can create a simple electric generator easily. All you need to do is create a simple frame to hold the wire and magnet, wind the wire, connect it to an electrical device, and glue the magnet onto a spinning shaft. This even works well to teach electromagnetic properties, or display as a science project.
[[Category:Electrical Projects]]
[[Category:Motors Generators and Transformers]]
== Steps ==
===Building the Frame===

#Cut the cardboard. Cardboard will serve as the frame and support for your simple generator. Use a ruler to measure a cardboard strip that is {{convert|8|cm|in}} by {{convert|30.4|cm|in|}}. Cut this strip out with scissors or a utility knife. This single piece will be folded to form the frame.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 1 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Mark the cardboard. Use a ruler to measure along the length of the cardboard. Make your first mark at {{convert|8|cm|in}}. Your second mark should be at {{convert|11.5|cm|in}}, and your third mark should be at {{convert|19.5|cm|in}}. The final mark will be at {{convert|22.7|cm|in}}.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 2 Version 4.jpg|center]]
#*This creates segments of {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.5|cm|in}}, {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.2|cm|in}}, and {{convert|7.7|cm|in}}. Do not cut these segments.

#Fold the cardboard. Fold the cardboard along each mark. This will make your flat piece of cardboard into a rectangular frame. This frame will house the components of your electric motor.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 3 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Slide the metal shaft through the support frame. Push a nail through the center of the cardboard frame. Make sure you go through all three pieces of cardboard that are folded into the center. This will create the hole for your shaft. You can now insert a metal shaft, or use the nail as your shaft.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#07</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 4 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#*The metal shaft does not have to be anything in particular. Any piece of metal that will fit through the hole and come all the way out the other side of the frame is acceptable. The nail you use to make the hole will work perfectly.
===Creating the Circuit===

#Wind the copper wire. Make several turns around the cardboard box with enamel coated copper wire (#30 magnet wire). Wind {{convert|200|ft|m|}} of wire as tight as you can. Leave about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your meter, light bulb, or other electronic device. The more "turns" or winds you make around the cardboard frame, the more power your generator should produce.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 5 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Strip the ends of the wire. Use a knife or a wire stripper to remove the insulation from each end of the wire. Remove about {{convert|2.54|cm|in|}} of insulation from each side. This will allow you to connect the wire to an electronic device.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 6 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Connect the wires to an electronic device. Attach the two wires you have loose at the ends of the windings to a red LED, #49 miniature bulb, or a 1.5V grain-of-wheat lamp. Or, connect the test leads from an AC voltmeter or multimeter to them. Keep in mind that you are producing a very low voltage, and larger devices (e.g. a regular light bulb) will not be powered by this generator.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 7 Version 5.jpg|center]]
===Setting the Magnets===

#Glue the magnets to the shaft. Use a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy to glue four ceramic magnets to the shaft. You want the magnet to be stationary with respect to the shaft. The magnets should be glued onto the shaft after the shaft has been inserted into the frame. Allow the glue to dry for several minutes (the instructions on the container can tell you exact drying times for your type of glue).<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 8 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*For best results, use 1x2x5 cm ceramic magnets (these can be found online for a reasonable price). Glue them so that two magnets are facing the coil with their north side, and two are facing the coil with their south side.

#Turn the shaft with your fingers. This allows you to see if the ends of the magnets hit the inside of the frame. The magnets must turn freely, but as close as possible to the walls of the frame. Again, having the magnet's ends as close the copper wire windings as possible will increase the "exciting" action of the magnetic fields the magnet produces.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 9 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Spin the shaft as fast as possible. You may want to wind a string around the end of the shaft, then pull it sharply to turn the magnets. You could even just spin it with your fingers. As the shaft turns, you should get a small voltage (enough to light a 1.5 volt light bulb).<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 10 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*You could improve the power output by putting a pinwheel on the end of the shaft and connecting it to an electric fan to turn the wheel. Keep in mind that this is only good to demonstrate the operation of the generator since you use more electricity turning it than you create.

{{Video:Make a Simple Electric Generator|}}
== Things You'll Need ==
* #30 Magnet wire
* Four 1x2x5 cm ceramic magnets
* Thick nail or shaft
* Cardboard box
* Multimeter or electrical device

removed: Electric generators are devices that use alternating magnetic fields to create a current through a wire circuit. While full scale models can be complex and expensive to build, you can create a simple electric generator easily. All you need to do is create a simple frame to hold the wire and magnet, wind the wire, connect it to an electrical device, and glue the magnet onto a spinning shaft. This even works well to teach electromagnetic properties, or display as a science project.
[[Category:Electrical Projects]]
[[Category:Motors Generators and Transformers]]
== Steps ==
===Building the Frame===

#Cut the cardboard. Cardboard will serve as the frame and support for your simple generator. Use a ruler to measure a cardboard strip that is {{convert|8|cm|in}} by {{convert|30.4|cm|in|}}. Cut this strip out with scissors or a utility knife. This single piece will be folded to form the frame.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 1 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Mark the cardboard. Use a ruler to measure along the length of the cardboard. Make your first mark at {{convert|8|cm|in}}. Your second mark should be at {{convert|11.5|cm|in}}, and your third mark should be at {{convert|19.5|cm|in}}. The final mark will be at {{convert|22.7|cm|in}}.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 2 Version 4.jpg|center]]
#*This creates segments of {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.5|cm|in}}, {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.2|cm|in}}, and {{convert|7.7|cm|in}}. Do not cut these segments.

#Fold the cardboard. Fold the cardboard along each mark. This will make your flat piece of cardboard into a rectangular frame. This frame will house the components of your electric motor.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 3 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Slide the metal shaft through the support frame. Push a nail through the center of the cardboard frame. Make sure you go through all three pieces of cardboard that are folded into the center. This will create the hole for your shaft. You can now insert a metal shaft, or use the nail as your shaft.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#07</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 4 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#*The metal shaft does not have to be anything in particular. Any piece of metal that will fit through the hole and come all the way out the other side of the frame is acceptable. The nail you use to make the hole will work perfectly.
===Creating the Circuit===

#Wind the copper wire. Make several turns around the cardboard box with enamel coated copper wire (#30 magnet wire). Wind {{convert|200|ft|m|}} of wire as tight as you can. Leave about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your meter, light bulb, or other electronic device. The more "turns" or winds you make around the cardboard frame, the more power your generator should produce.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 5 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Strip the ends of the wire. Use a knife or a wire stripper to remove the insulation from each end of the wire. Remove about {{convert|2.54|cm|in|}} of insulation from each side. This will allow you to connect the wire to an electronic device.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 6 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Connect the wires to an electronic device. Attach the two wires you have loose at the ends of the windings to a red LED, #49 miniature bulb, or a 1.5V grain-of-wheat lamp. Or, connect the test leads from an AC voltmeter or multimeter to them. Keep in mind that you are producing a very low voltage, and larger devices (e.g. a regular light bulb) will not be powered by this generator.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 7 Version 5.jpg|center]]
===Setting the Magnets===

#Glue the magnets to the shaft. Use a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy to glue four ceramic magnets to the shaft. You want the magnet to be stationary with respect to the shaft. The magnets should be glued onto the shaft after the shaft has been inserted into the frame. Allow the glue to dry for several minutes (the instructions on the container can tell you exact drying times for your type of glue).<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 8 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*For best results, use 1x2x5 cm ceramic magnets (these can be found online for a reasonable price). Glue them so that two magnets are facing the coil with their north side, and two are facing the coil with their south side.

#Turn the shaft with your fingers. This allows you to see if the ends of the magnets hit the inside of the frame. The magnets must turn freely, but as close as possible to the walls of the frame. Again, having the magnet's ends as close the copper wire windings as possible will increase the "exciting" action of the magnetic fields the magnet produces.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 9 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Spin the shaft as fast as possible. You may want to wind a string around the end of the shaft, then pull it sharply to turn the magnets. You could even just spin it with your fingers. As the shaft turns, you should get a small voltage (enough to light a 1.5 volt light bulb).<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 10 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*You could improve the power output by putting a pinwheel on the end of the shaft and connecting it to an electric fan to turn the wheel. Keep in mind that this is only good to demonstrate the operation of the generator since you use more electricity turning it than you create.

added: Electric generators are devices that use alternating magnetic fields to create a current through a wire circuit. While full scale models can be complex and expensive to build, you can create a simple electric generator easily. All you need to do is create a simple frame to hold the wire and magnet, wind the wire, connect it to an electrical device, and glue the magnet onto a spinning shaft. This even works well to teach electromagnetic properties, or display as a science project.
[[Category:Motors Generators and Transformers]]
[[Category:Electrical Projects]]
== Steps ==
===Building the Frame===

#Cut the cardboard. Cardboard will serve as the frame and support for your simple generator. Use a ruler to measure a cardboard strip that is {{convert|8|cm|in}} by {{convert|30.4|cm|in|}}. Cut this strip out with scissors or a utility knife. This single piece will be folded to form the frame.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 1 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Mark the cardboard. Use a ruler to measure along the length of the cardboard. Make your first mark at {{convert|8|cm|in}}. Your second mark should be at {{convert|11.5|cm|in}}, and your third mark should be at {{convert|19.5|cm|in}}. The final mark will be at {{convert|22.7|cm|in}}.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 2 Version 4.jpg|center]]
#*This creates segments of {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.5|cm|in}}, {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.2|cm|in}}, and {{convert|7.7|cm|in}}. Do not cut these segments.

#Fold the cardboard. Fold the cardboard along each mark. This will make your flat piece of cardboard into a rectangular frame. This frame will house the components of your electric motor.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 3 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Slide the metal shaft through the support frame. Push a nail through the center of the cardboard frame. Make sure you go through all three pieces of cardboard that are folded into the center. This will create the hole for your shaft. You can now insert a metal shaft, or use the nail as your shaft.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#07</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 4 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#*The metal shaft does not have to be anything in particular. Any piece of metal that will fit through the hole and come all the way out the other side of the frame is acceptable. The nail you use to make the hole will work perfectly.
===Creating the Circuit===

#Wind the copper wire. Make several turns around the cardboard box with enamel coated copper wire (#30 magnet wire). Wind {{convert|200|ft|m|}} of wire as tight as you can. Leave about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your meter, light bulb, or other electronic device. The more "turns" or winds you make around the cardboard frame, the more power your generator should produce.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 5 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Strip the ends of the wire. Use a knife or a wire stripper to remove the insulation from each end of the wire. Remove about {{convert|2.54|cm|in|}} of insulation from each side. This will allow you to connect the wire to an electronic device.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 6 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Connect the wires to an electronic device. Attach the two wires you have loose at the ends of the windings to a red LED, #49 miniature bulb, or a 1.5V grain-of-wheat lamp. Or, connect the test leads from an AC voltmeter or multimeter to them. Keep in mind that you are producing a very low voltage, and larger devices (e.g. a regular light bulb) will not be powered by this generator.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 7 Version 5.jpg|center]]
===Setting the Magnets===

#Glue the magnets to the shaft. Use a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy to glue four ceramic magnets to the shaft. You want the magnet to be stationary with respect to the shaft. The magnets should be glued onto the shaft after the shaft has been inserted into the frame. Allow the glue to dry for several minutes (the instructions on the container can tell you exact drying times for your type of glue).<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 8 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*For best results, use 1x2x5 cm ceramic magnets (these can be found online for a reasonable price). Glue them so that two magnets are facing the coil with their north side, and two are facing the coil with their south side.

#Turn the shaft with your fingers. This allows you to see if the ends of the magnets hit the inside of the frame. The magnets must turn freely, but as close as possible to the walls of the frame. Again, having the magnet's ends as close the copper wire windings as possible will increase the "exciting" action of the magnetic fields the magnet produces.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 9 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Spin the shaft as fast as possible. You may want to wind a string around the end of the shaft, then pull it sharply to turn the magnets. You could even just spin it with your fingers. As the shaft turns, you should get a small voltage (enough to light a 1.5 volt light bulb).<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 10 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*You could improve the power output by putting a pinwheel on the end of the shaft and connecting it to an electric fan to turn the wheel. Keep in mind that this is only good to demonstrate the operation of the generator since you use more electricity turning it than you create.

added: Electric generators are devices that use alternating magnetic fields to create a current through a wire circuit. While full scale models can be complex and expensive to build, you can create a simple electric generator easily. All you need to do is create a simple frame to hold the wire and magnet, wind the wire, connect it to an electrical device, and glue the magnet onto a spinning shaft. This even works well to teach electromagnetic properties, or display as a science project.
[[Category:Motors Generators and Transformers]]
[[Category:Electrical Projects]]
== Steps ==
===Building the Frame===

#Cut the cardboard. Cardboard will serve as the frame and support for your simple generator. Use a ruler to measure a cardboard strip that is {{convert|8|cm|in}} by {{convert|30.4|cm|in|}}. Cut this strip out with scissors or a utility knife. This single piece will be folded to form the frame.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 1 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Mark the cardboard. Use a ruler to measure along the length of the cardboard. Make your first mark at {{convert|8|cm|in}}. Your second mark should be at {{convert|11.5|cm|in}}, and your third mark should be at {{convert|19.5|cm|in}}. The final mark will be at {{convert|22.7|cm|in}}.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 2 Version 4.jpg|center]]
#*This creates segments of {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.5|cm|in}}, {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.2|cm|in}}, and {{convert|7.7|cm|in}}. Do not cut these segments.

#Fold the cardboard. Fold the cardboard along each mark. This will make your flat piece of cardboard into a rectangular frame. This frame will house the components of your electric motor.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 3 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Slide the metal shaft through the support frame. Push a nail through the center of the cardboard frame. Make sure you go through all three pieces of cardboard that are folded into the center. This will create the hole for your shaft. You can now insert a metal shaft, or use the nail as your shaft.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#07</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 4 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#*The metal shaft does not have to be anything in particular. Any piece of metal that will fit through the hole and come all the way out the other side of the frame is acceptable. The nail you use to make the hole will work perfectly.
===Creating the Circuit===

#Wind the copper wire. Make several turns around the cardboard box with enamel coated copper wire (#30 magnet wire). Wind {{convert|200|ft|m|}} of wire as tight as you can. Leave about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your meter, light bulb, or other electronic device. The more "turns" or winds you make around the cardboard frame, the more power your generator should produce.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 5 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Strip the ends of the wire. Use a knife or a wire stripper to remove the insulation from each end of the wire. Remove about {{convert|2.54|cm|in|}} of insulation from each side. This will allow you to connect the wire to an electronic device.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 6 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Connect the wires to an electronic device. Attach the two wires you have loose at the ends of the windings to a red LED, #49 miniature bulb, or a 1.5V grain-of-wheat lamp. Or, connect the test leads from an AC voltmeter or multimeter to them. Keep in mind that you are producing a very low voltage, and larger devices (e.g. a regular light bulb) will not be powered by this generator.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 7 Version 5.jpg|center]]
===Setting the Magnets===

#Glue the magnets to the shaft. Use a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy to glue four ceramic magnets to the shaft. You want the magnet to be stationary with respect to the shaft. The magnets should be glued onto the shaft after the shaft has been inserted into the frame. Allow the glue to dry for several minutes (the instructions on the container can tell you exact drying times for your type of glue).<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 8 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*For best results, use 1x2x5 cm ceramic magnets (these can be found online for a reasonable price). Glue them so that two magnets are facing the coil with their north side, and two are facing the coil with their south side.

#Turn the shaft with your fingers. This allows you to see if the ends of the magnets hit the inside of the frame. The magnets must turn freely, but as close as possible to the walls of the frame. Again, having the magnet's ends as close the copper wire windings as possible will increase the "exciting" action of the magnetic fields the magnet produces.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 9 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Spin the shaft as fast as possible. You may want to wind a string around the end of the shaft, then pull it sharply to turn the magnets. You could even just spin it with your fingers. As the shaft turns, you should get a small voltage (enough to light a 1.5 volt light bulb).<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 10 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*You could improve the power output by putting a pinwheel on the end of the shaft and connecting it to an electric fan to turn the wheel. Keep in mind that this is only good to demonstrate the operation of the generator since you use more electricity turning it than you create.

Your second mark should be at {{convert|11.5|cm|in}}, and your third mark should be at {{convert|19.5|cm|in}}. The final mark will be at {{convert|22.7|cm|in}}.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 2 Version 4.jpg|center]]
#*This creates segments of {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.5|cm|in}}, {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.2|cm|in}}, and {{convert|7.7|cm|in}}. Do not cut these segments.

#Fold the cardboard. Fold the cardboard along each mark. This will make your flat piece of cardboard into a rectangular frame. This frame will house the components of your electric motor.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 3 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Slide the metal shaft through the support frame. Push a nail through the center of the cardboard frame. Make sure you go through all three pieces of cardboard that are folded into the center. This will create the hole for your shaft. You can now insert a metal shaft, or use the nail as your shaft.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#07</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 4 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#*The metal shaft does not have to be anything in particular. Any piece of metal that will fit through the hole and come all the way out the other side of the frame is acceptable. The nail you use to make the hole will work perfectly.

#Wind the copper wire. Make several turns around the cardboard box with enamel coated copper wire (#30 magnet wire). Wind {{convert|200|ft|m|}} of wire as tight as you can. Leave about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your meter, light bulb, or other electronic device. Or, connect the test leads from an AC voltmeter or multimeter to them. #Glue the magnets to the shaft. pinUse a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy to glue four ceramic magnets to the shaft. You want the magnet to be stationary with respect to the shaft. The magnets should be glued onto the shaft after the shaft has been inserted into the frame. Allow the glue to dry for several minutes (the instructions on the container can tell you exact drying times for your type of glue).<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 8 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#*For best results, use 1x2x5 cm ceramic magnets (these can be found online for a reasonable price). Glue them so that two magnets are facing the coil with their north side, and two are facing the coil with their south side.

You can now insert a metal shaft, or use the nail as your shaft.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#07</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 4 Version 4.jpg|center]]

You can now insert a metal shaft, or use the nail as your shaft.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#07</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 4 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Wind the copper wire. Make several turns around the cardboard box with enamel coated copper wire (#30 magnet wire). Wind {{convert|200|ft|m|}} of wire as tight as you can. Leave about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your meter, light bulb, or other electronic device. The more "turns" or winds you make around the cardboard frame, the more power your generator should produce.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 5 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Strip the ends of the wire. Use a knife or a wire stripper to remove the insulation from each end of the wire. Remove about {{convert|2.54|cm|in|}} of insulation from each side. This will allow you to connect the wire to an electronic device.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 6 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Connect the wires to an electronic device. Attach the two wires you have loose at the ends of the windings to a red LED, #49 miniature bulb, or a 1.5V grain-of-wheat lamp. Or, connect the test leads from an AC voltmeter or multimeter to them. Keep in mind that you are producing a very low voltage, and larger devices (e.g. a regular light bulb) will not be powered by this generator.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 7 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Glue the magnets to the shaft. Use a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy to glue four ceramic magnets to the shaft. You want the magnet to be stationary with respect to the shaft. The magnets should be glued onto the shaft after the shaft has been inserted into the frame. Allow the glue to dry for several minutes (the instructions on the container can tell you exact drying times for your type of glue).<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 8 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Turn the shaft with your fingers. This allows you to see if the ends of the magnets hit the inside of the frame. The magnets must turn freely, but as close as possible to the walls of the frame. Again, having the magnet's ends as close the copper wire windings as possible will increase the "exciting" action of the magnetic fields the magnet produces.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 9 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Spin the shaft as fast as possible. You may want to wind a string around the end of the shaft, then pull it sharply to turn the magnets. You could even just spin it with your fingers. As the shaft turns, you should get a small voltage (enough to light a 1.5 volt light bulb).<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 10 Version 5.jpg|center]]

added: Electric generators are devices that use alternating magnetic fields to create a current through a wire circuit. While full scale models can be complex and expensive to build, you can create a simple electric generator easily. All you need to do is create a simple frame to hold the wire and magnet, wind the wire, connect it to an electrical device, and glue the magnet onto a spinning shaft. This even works well to teach electromagnetic properties, or display as a science project.

#Wind the copper wire. Make several turns around the cardboard box with enamel coated copper wire (#30 magnet wire). Wind {{convert|200|ft|m|}} of wire as tight as you can. Leave about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your meter, light bulb, or other electronic device. The more "turns" or winds you make around the cardboard frame, the more power your generator should produce.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>

#Glue the magnets to the shaft. Use a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy to glue four ceramic magnets to the shaft. You want the magnet to be stationary with respect to the shaft. The magnets should be glued onto the shaft after the shaft has been inserted into the frame. Allow the glue to dry for several minutes (the instructions on the container can tell you exact drying times for your type of glue).<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>

#*For best results, use 1x2x5 cm ceramic magnets (these can be found online for a reasonable price). Glue them so that two magnets are facing the coil with their north side, and two are facing the coil with their south side.

#*You could improve the power output by putting a pinwheel on the end of the shaft and connecting it to an electric fan to turn the wheel. Keep in mind that this is only good to demonstrate the operation of the generator since you use more electricity turning it than you create.
* #30 Magnet wire
* Four 1x2x5 cm ceramic magnets
* Thick nail or shaft
* Cardboard box
* Multimeter or electrical device

== Tips ==
*You may want to fashion a small pulley and attach an electric motor to the shaft to produce enough RPMs to maintain an electric current.
*Don't use vinyl-insulated wire.   The insulation must be very thin:  enamel-coated wire, called "magnet wire."

*26-32 ga. insulated or enameled copper wire. About {{convert|25|ft|m|1}} will produce a modest electrical current. More "windings", and larger wire, coupled with a stronger magnet will increase the power output.
*{{convert|3|or|4|in|cm|adj=on|1}} steel bar magnet. (Should fit lengthwise in the cardboard tube, below, with a little clearance)
*{{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} diameter rod, metal, wood, or plastic {{convert|12|in|cm|1}} in length.
*{{convert|24|in|cm|1}} of 1X4 lumber
*{{convert|4|in|cm|adj=on|1}} paper or cardboard tube
*2 {{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1}} flat washers

===Building the Frame===

#Cut the cardboard. Cardboard will serve as the frame and support for your simple generator. Cut a cardboard strip that is {{convert|8|cm|in}} by {{convert|30.4|cm|in|}}. This single piece will be folded to form the frame.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>

#Mark the cardboard. Use a ruler to measure along the length of the cardboard. Make your first mark at {{convert|8|cm|in}}. Your second mark should be at {{convert|11.5|cm|in}}, and your third mark should be at {{convert|19.5|cm|in}}. The final mark will be at {{convert|22.7|cm|in}}.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>
#*This creates segments of {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.5|cm|in}}, {{convert|8|cm|in}}, {{convert|3.2|cm|in}}, and {{convert|7.7|cm|in}}. Do not cut these segments.

#Fold the cardboard. Fold the cardboard along each mark. This will make your flat piece of cardboard into a rectangular frame. This frame will house the components of your electric motor.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>

#Slide the metal shaft through the support frame. Push a nail through the center of the cardboard frame. Make sure you go through all three pieces of cardboard that are folded into the center. This will create the hole for your shaft. You can now insert a metal shaft, or use the nail as your shaft.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#07</ref>
===Creating the Circuit===

#Wind the copper wire. Make several turns around the cardboard box with the copper wire. Leave about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your meter, light bulb, or other electronic device. The more "turns" or winds you make around the cardboard frame, the more power your generator should produce.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>

#Strip the ends of the wire. Use a knife or a wire stripper to remove the insulation from each end of the wire. Remove about {{convert|2.54|cm|in|}} of insulation from each side. This will allow you to connect the wire to an electronic device.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>

#Connect the wires to an electronic device. Attach the two wires you have loose at the ends of the windings to a red LED, #49 miniature bulb, or a 1.5V grain-of-wheat lamp. Or, connect the test leads from an AC voltmeter or multimeter to them. Keep in mind that you are producing a very low voltage, and larger devices (e.g. a regular light bulb) will not be powered by this generator.<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>
===Setting the Magnets===

#Glue the magnets to the shaft. Use a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy. You want the magnet to be stationary with respect to the shaft. The magnets should be glued onto the shaft after the shaft has been inserted into the frame..<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>

#Turn the shaft with your fingers. This allows you to see if the ends of the magnets hit the inside of the frame. The magnets must turn freely, but as close as possible to the walls of the frame. Again, having the magnet's ends as close the copper wire windings as possible will increase the "exciting" action of the magnetic fields the magnet produces.<ref>http://amasci.com/coilgen/generator_1.html</ref>

#Spin the shaft as fast as possible. You may want to wind a string around the end of the shaft, then pull it sharply to turn the magnets. You could even just spin it with your fingers. As the shaft turns, you should get a small voltage (enough to light a 1.5 volt light bulb).<ref>http://www.bigshotcamera.com/fun/buildables/generator#01</ref>

#Decide how large a project you are interested in building. There are design and engineering considerations that could be taken up, but for simplicity's sake, this article will give instructions for a simple, low output generator.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 1 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Acquire the materials you will need. The sizes and specifications can be adjusted to raise the output capacity of your generator, but this is a basic overview of the project.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 2 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*22-32 ga. enameled copper wire. About {{convert|500|ft|m|1}} will produce a modest electrical current. More "windings", coupled with a stronger magnet will increase the voltage output.
#*{{convert|3|or|4|in|cm|adj=on|1}} steel bar magnet. (Should fit lengthwise in the cardboard tube, below, with a little clearance.)
#*{{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} diameter rod, metal, plastic or wood {{convert|12|in|cm|1}} in length.
#*{{convert|24|in|cm|1}} of 1X4 lumber.
#*1 - large paper or cardboard tube, {{convert|4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} diameter.
#*2 - {{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} flat washers.
#Build a "U" shaped frame to support your "rotor", ie, the permanent bar magnet mounted on a steel shaft.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 3 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*Cut the 1X4 lumber into pieces, 2, at {{convert|6|in|cm|adj=on|1}} lengths, one at {{convert|12|in|cm|1}} in length.

#*Nail or screw the two {{convert|6|in|cm|adj=on|1}} boards to the {{convert|12|in|cm|adj=on|1}} board at a perpendicular angle to the {{convert|12|in|cm|adj=on|1}} board, which is the base for the rotor frame.

#Drill two {{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} holes in the two uprights of your frame. Align them so that the {{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} rod, (the rotor shaft) will go through both without binding.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 4 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Drill a {{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} hole through the center of your steel bar magnet, on the flat, or widest side. Be careful to measure the center both in length and width, and drill perpendicularly, so that when the shaft goes through, the magnet will be "square" to the shaft.  (Only drill through steel magnets, not other types.)[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 5 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#Slide the metal shaft through one side of the support frame, slide the magnet onto the shaft.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 6 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Cut a {{convert|4|in|cm|adj=on|1}} section of the paper or cardboard tube. If you don't have a piece of tubing available, you can make one by rolling a sheet of construction paper into a cylinder and gluing or taping it to secure it in this shape. The ideal diameter of the tube will be just large enough to allow the bar magnet to spin freely inside the tube, keeping the magnetic field as near the copper windings as possible.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 7 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Wind the copper wire around the cardboard or paper tube, leaving about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your power test device, an electric light bulb, or other device you will supply power to. The more "turns" or winds around the tube you make, the more power your generator should produce.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 8 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Slide the tube over the shaft and magnet, then slide the shaft on through the other support frame. You will want several inches of the shaft sticking through each end of the frame.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 9 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Glue the magnet to the shaft at the center of the two supports, using a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy. You may choose to drill and tap threads into the magnet for a "set screw" if you have the tools to do so, but the idea is for the magnet to be stationary in relation to the shaft. This will be inside of the paper tube later on.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 10 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Support the paper cylinder with the wire windings at the center of the shaft with the bar magnet centered on the wire windings. You may simply cut cardboard legs that can be glued to the cylinder, or build a wire frame from a coat hanger or similar stiff wire to accomplish this.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 11 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Turn the shaft with your fingers to see if the ends of the magnet hit the inside of the tube. It must turn freely, but not as close as possible to the tube. Again, having the magnet's ends as close the copper wire windings will increase the "exciting" action of the magnetic fields the magnet produces.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 12 Version 4.jpg|center]]
#Glue a washer on each end of the shaft outside the wood supports.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 13 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Attach the two wires you have loose at the ends of the windings to a red LED, #49 miniature bulb, or a 1.5V grain-of-wheat lamp.  Or, connect the test leads from an AC voltmeter or multimeter to them.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 14 Version 4.jpg|center]]

#Spin the shaft as fast as possible. You may want to wind a string around the end of the shaft as you would a toy "top", then pull it sharply, or just spin it with your fingers. You should get a small voltage, enough to light a 1.5 volt light bulb by manually spinning the shaft[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 15 Version 4.jpg|center]]
*Rather than drilling through a magnet, instead clamp a small spacer (a piece of wood or plastic) between two magnets, then drill through this spacer.
== Warnings ==

*Only drill old-style steel magnets.  '''Modern magnets cannot be drilled.''' Rare earth super magnets  can burst into flame during attempted drilling.   Ceramic magnets are harder than metal, and will just ruin your drill.
*Electric drill
*Saw

#Slide the metal shaft through one side of the support frame, slide the magnet onto the shaft.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 6 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Cut a {{convert|4|in|cm|adj=on|1}} section of the paper or cardboard tube. If you don't have a piece of tubing available, you can make one by rolling a sheet of construction paper into a cylinder and gluing or taping it to secure it in this shape. The ideal diameter of the tube will be just large enough to allow the bar magnet to spin freely inside the tube, keeping the magnetic field as near the copper windings as possible.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 7 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Wind the copper wire around the cardboard or paper tube, leaving about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your power test device, an electric light bulb, or other device you will supply power to. The more "turns" or winds around the tube you make, the more power your generator should produce.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 8 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Slide the tube over the shaft and magnet, then slide the shaft on through the other support frame. You will want several inches of the shaft sticking through each end of the frame.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 9 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Glue the magnet to the shaft at the center of the two supports, using a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy. You may choose to drill and tap threads into the magnet for a "set screw" if you have the tools to do so, but the idea is for the magnet to be stationary in relation to the shaft. This will be inside of the paper tube later on.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 10 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Support the paper cylinder with the wire windings at the center of the shaft with the bar magnet centered on the wire windings. You may simply cut cardboard legs that can be glued to the cylinder, or build a wire frame from a coat hanger or similar stiff wire to accomplish this.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 11 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Turn the shaft with your fingers to see if the ends of the magnet hit the inside of the tube. It must turn freely, but not as close as possible to the tube. Again, having the magnet's ends as close the copper wire windings will increase the "exciting" action of the magnetic fields the magnet produces.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 12 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#Glue a washer on each end of the shaft outside the wood supports.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 13 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Attach the two wires you have loose at the ends of the windings to a red LED, #49 miniature bulb, or a 1.5V grain-of-wheat lamp.  Or, connect the test leads from an AC voltmeter or multimeter to them.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 14 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Spin the shaft as fast as possible. You may want to wind a string around the end of the shaft as you would a toy "top", then pull it sharply, or just spin it with your fingers. You should get a small voltage, enough to light a 1.5 volt light bulb by manually spinning the shaft[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 15 Version 3.jpg|center]]

added: #Decide how large a project you are interested in building. There are design and engineering considerations that could be taken up, but for simplicity's sake, this article will give instructions for a simple, low output generator.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 1 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Acquire the materials you will need. The sizes and specifications can be adjusted to raise the output capacity of your generator, but this is a basic overview of the project.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*22-28 ga. enameled copper wire. About {{convert|500|ft|m|1}} will produce a modest electrical current. More "windings", coupled with a stronger magnet will increase the power output.
#*{{convert|3|or|4|in|cm|adj=on|1}} bar magnet. (Should fit lengthwise in the cardboard tube, below, with a little clearance)
#*{{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} diameter steel or aluminum rod, {{convert|12|in|cm|1}} in length.
#*{{convert|24|in|cm|1}} of 1X4 lumber.
#*1 - large paper or cardboard tube, 4-inch (10-cm) diameter.
#*2 - 1/4 inch (5.7 cm) flat washers.
#Build a "U" shaped frame to support your "rotor", ie, the permanent bar magnet mounted on a steel shaft. by[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 3 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*Cut the 1X4 lumber into pieces, 2, at {{convert|6|in|cm|adj=on|1}} lengths, one at {{convert|12|in|cm|1}} in length.

#*Nail or screw the two {{convert|6|in|cm|adj=on|1}} boards to the {{convert|12|in|cm|adj=on|1}} board at a perpendicular angle to the {{convert|12|in|cm|adj=on|1}} board, which is the base for the rotor frame.

#Drill two {{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} holes in the two uprights of your frame, aligning them so that the {{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} rod, (the rotor shaft) will go through both without binding.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 4 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Drill a {{convert|1/4|in|cm|adj=on|1|1}} hole through the center of your bar magnet, on the flat, or widest side. Be careful to measure the center both in length and width, and drill perpendicularly, so that when the shaft goes through, the magnet will be "square" to the shaft.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#Slide the metal shaft through one side of the support frame, slide the magnet onto the shaft.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 6 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Cut a {{convert|4|in|cm|adj=on|1}} section of the paper or cardboard tube. If you don't have a piece of tubing available, you can make one by rolling a sheet of construction paper into a cylinder and gluing or taping it to secure it in this shape. The ideal diameter of the tube will be just large enough to allow the bar magnet to spin freely inside the tube, keeping the magnetic field as near the copper windings as possible.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 7 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Wind the copper wire around the cardboard or paper tube, leaving about {{convert|16|to|18|in|cm|1}} of wire loose on each end to connect to your power test device, an electric light bulb, or other device you will supply power to. The more "turns" or winds around the tube you make, the more power your generator should produce.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 8 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Slide the tube over the shaft and magnet, then slide the shaft on through the other support frame. You will want several inches of the shaft sticking through each end of the frame.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 9 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Glue the magnet to the shaft at the center of the two supports, using a high strength hot melt glue or epoxy. You may choose to drill and tap threads into the magnet for a "set screw" if you have the tools to do so, but the idea is for the magnet to be stationary in relation to the shaft.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 10 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Support the paper cylinder with the wire windings at the center of the shaft with the bar magnet centered on the wire windings. You may simply cut cardboard legs that can be glued to the cylinder, or build a wire frame from a coat hanger or similar stiff wire to accomplish this.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 11 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Turn the shaft with your fingers to see if the ends of the magnet hit the inside of the tube. It must turn freely, but be as close as possible to the tube. Again, having the magnet's ends as close the copper wire windings will increase the "exciting" action of the magnetic fields the magnet produces.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 12 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#Glue a washer on each end of the shaft outside the wood supports.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 13 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Attach the two wires you have loose at the ends of the windings to a flashlight bulb or other low voltage lamp, or connect the test leads from a voltmeter or multimeter to them.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 14 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Spin the shaft as fast as possible. You may want to wind a string around the end of the shaft as you would a toy "top", then pull it sharply, or just spin it with your fingers. You should get a small voltage, enough to light a 1.5 volt light bulb by manually spinning the shaft.[[Image:Make a Simple Electric Generator Step 15 Version 2.jpg|center]]
